nameStory: The eastern red bat gets its name from the male's gorgeous rusty-red fur that glows like autumn leaves in sunlight. Females are actually more brownish-orange, but the fiery males made such an impression that they gave the whole species its common name.
description: The eastern red bat is a medium-sized bat with distinctly colorful fur that sets it apart from most other North American bats. Males sport bright rusty-red coats while females are more brownish-orange with a frosted appearance from white-tipped hairs. These solitary bats typically measure 3-5 inches long with a wingspan of 11-13 inches, making them one of the more noticeable bats when spotted.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Males have brilliant rusty-red fur that feels soft and dense, while females are brownish-orange with white-frosted tips that give them a silvery sheen in sunlight

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized with broad, triangular ears and a distinctly hairy tail membrane that extends all the way to the tip - you can actually see the fur covering it

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Roosts alone in tree foliage rather than in colonies, hanging like a dead leaf 3-40 feet up, and flies with distinctly erratic, moth-like wingbeats

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: The only bat you're likely to find roosting in deciduous tree leaves during the day, often in edge habitats where woods meet fields

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Look for small, dark droppings about the size of rice grains beneath roosting trees, often accumulated in small piles

habitat: Eastern red bats prefer wooded areas throughout New England, especially forest edges, parks, and suburban areas with mature deciduous trees. They roost in the foliage of trees like oaks, maples, and sycamores, typically 3-40 feet off the ground. You'll find them anywhere there are insects to hunt and leafy trees for daytime shelter, from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Active from April onward as they return from southern wintering grounds, often seen hunting insects around streetlights and forest clearings in early evening.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're raising young and most easily observed. Pregnant females give birth to 1-5 pups in June, and family groups may roost together briefly.
seasonality.fall: Begin migration south in late August through October. This is when you're most likely to spot them as they gather in larger numbers before departing.
seasonality.winter: Most migrate south to warmer climates, though a few may hibernate in leaf litter or tree hollows during mild winters in southern New England.

funFact: Eastern red bats are one of the few bat species where mothers regularly carry their babies while flying - imagine a mom bat with up to four pups clinging to her fur as she hunts for insects in the night sky!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with big brown bats, but red bats have much more colorful fur and always roost alone in tree leaves rather than in buildings or bat boxes. Remember: red fur = red bat, and if it's hanging solo in a tree, you've found your species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite the name 'eastern' red bat, these animals are actually found across much of North America. The 'eastern' refers to the fact that they were first scientifically described from eastern populations, distinguishing them from western bat species.
compareHints: Eastern red bats are much smaller and more colorful than their cousin the northern hoary bat, which is larger with distinctive white-frosted fur all over. Red bats also prefer deciduous trees while hoary bats often roost in conifers. Both species are solitary roosters, unlike most other New England bats that form colonies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: While the Eastern Red Bat (its closest New England relative in the same genus) has distinctive rusty-red fur and roosts in dense foliage, the Northern Hoary Bat's frosted silver appearance and larger size make it unmistakable.
